question: What are hooks and why were they introduced?
shortAnswer: Hooks are functions starting with use that let function components hold state and tap into React features. They were introduced to solve logic reuse: before hooks, sharing stateful logic meant higher-order components or render props, which produced deeply nested wrapper trees. A custom hook shares logic without touching the component hierarchy at all.
memoryHook: Hooks let you extract stateful logic without adding a component. HOCs shared logic by nesting; hooks share it by calling.

resources.title: react.dev — Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

question: What are the rules of hooks and why do they exist?
shortAnswer: Only call hooks at the top level of a component or another hook — never inside conditions, loops or nested functions — and only from React functions, not plain JavaScript. The reason is that React identifies hooks by call order, not by name. Skip one conditionally and every subsequent hook shifts to the wrong slot.
memoryHook: React tracks hooks by position in the call order. An if statement around a hook shuffles the deck.

question: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
shortAnswer: useMemo caches the value a function returns; useCallback caches the function itself. useCallback(fn, deps) is exactly useMemo(() => fn, deps). You use useMemo for expensive calculations, and useCallback to keep a function's identity stable so a memoised child or an effect dependency does not fire needlessly.
memoryHook: useMemo remembers the RESULT, useCallback remembers the FUNCTION. Memo → value, Callback → callable.
answer:
## They are the same hook

```jsx
useCallback(fn, deps)
// is literally equivalent to
useMemo(() => fn, deps)
```

`useCallback` exists purely because caching a function is common enough to deserve less boilerplate.

---

## Side by side

```jsx
// useMemo — caches the returned VALUE
const sorted = useMemo(
  () => items.sort(byName),   // this runs; its result is cached
  [items]
);

// useCallback — caches the FUNCTION
const handleSelect = useCallback(
  (id) => setSelected(id),    // this does NOT run; the function itself is cached
  []
);
```

---

## When each is actually needed

**`useMemo`:**

| Reason | Example |
|--------|---------|
| Genuinely expensive calculation | Sorting 50,000 rows, parsing a large blob |
| Stable object/array identity for a memoised child | `const config = useMemo(() => ({ a, b }), [a, b])` |
| Stable context value | Prevents every consumer re-rendering |
| Stable effect dependency | Stops an effect firing every render |

**`useCallback`:**

| Reason | Example |
|--------|---------|
| Passing a handler to a `memo` child | Otherwise memo never bails out |
| Function in an effect's dependency array | Otherwise the effect re-runs every render |
| Returned from a custom hook | Consumers may depend on its identity |

---

## The mistake: memoising everything

```jsx
// ❌ Costs more than it saves
const doubled = useMemo(() => count * 2, [count]);
const onClick = useCallback(() => setOpen(true), []);   // passed to a plain <button>
```

Both hooks add real cost: an entry in the hook list, a dependency array to allocate and compare on every render. Multiplying two numbers is faster than checking whether you can skip multiplying two numbers.

**`useCallback` on a handler passed to a DOM element does nothing useful.** DOM elements are not memoised — React updates the listener either way.

---

## The critical caveat

```jsx
// ❌ Pointless — Child is not memoised, so it re-renders regardless
const handleClick = useCallback(() => {}, []);
return <Child onClick={handleClick} />;

// ✅ Now it has an effect
const Child = memo(function Child({ onClick }) { … });
```

`useCallback` only pays off if the receiver actually compares props. Memoising one prop while another changes identity every render is wasted work — this is the most common way memoisation gets applied without benefit.

> The **React Compiler** automates all of this. Where it is enabled, hand-written `useMemo` and `useCallback` largely become unnecessary.

question: What is useRef and what are its two distinct uses?
shortAnswer: useRef returns a mutable object with a current property that persists across renders and does not trigger a re-render when changed. Use it to reference a DOM node — focus, scroll, measure — or as an instance variable for values like timer ids and previous values that the UI does not display.
memoryHook: A box that survives re-renders but never causes one. State is for what you show; a ref is for what you remember.

question: What is useContext and what are its limitations?
shortAnswer: useContext reads the nearest matching Provider's value and subscribes the component to it. Its main limitation is that there are no selectors — every consumer re-renders when any part of the value changes, even a part it never reads. The second issue is that an inline object as the value creates a new reference each render, re-rendering all consumers unnecessarily.
memoryHook: Context has no selectors. Change one field and every consumer re-renders, even ones reading a different field.

question: How do you write a custom hook and what makes a good one?
shortAnswer: A custom hook is any function whose name starts with use and which calls other hooks. A good one has a single responsibility, returns a clear shape — a value, a tuple, or an object for three or more items — and handles its own cleanup. Each component that calls it gets completely independent state.
memoryHook: Custom hooks share logic, never data. Two components calling the same hook get two separate states.

question: What is useLayoutEffect and when should you use it instead of useEffect?
shortAnswer: useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after the DOM is updated but before the browser paints, whereas useEffect runs after paint. Use it only when you must measure the DOM and change it before the user sees anything, such as positioning a tooltip. Because it blocks painting, everything else should stay in useEffect.
memoryHook: Layout effect runs before paint and blocks it. Use it only to prevent a visible flicker.

question: What are useTransition and useDeferredValue?
shortAnswer: Both mark work as low priority so React can interrupt it to keep the UI responsive. useTransition wraps a state update you control and gives you an isPending flag. useDeferredValue takes a value you may not control — often a prop — and returns a lagging copy that renders at low priority. Use them when rendering is slow, not when the network is.
memoryHook: Transition wraps the UPDATE, deferred value wraps the VALUE. Both say: this can wait, keep typing.

question: What is useId and why can't you just use Math.random?
shortAnswer: useId generates a unique, stable id that matches between the server and client render, which is exactly what Math.random cannot do. It is for linking accessibility attributes like label htmlFor and aria-describedby to their targets. It is not for list keys — those must come from your data.
memoryHook: For accessibility ids that must survive SSR. Never for keys.

question: What is useImperativeHandle and when is it justified?
shortAnswer: useImperativeHandle customises what a parent receives when it puts a ref on your component, letting you expose specific methods instead of the raw DOM node. It is justified for imperative actions that genuinely cannot be expressed as state — focus, scroll into view, play, or resetting a third-party widget. Anything expressible as a prop should be a prop.
memoryHook: Expose verbs, not nouns. focus() and scrollIntoView() are fine; setValue() means you wanted a prop.

question: What is useSyncExternalStore for?
shortAnswer: It subscribes a component to a store that lives outside React — a Redux store, a browser API like navigator.onLine, or a custom event emitter — in a way that is safe under concurrent rendering. It prevents tearing, where two components render in the same pass but read different values because the store changed mid-render.
memoryHook: The safe way to read non-React state. Prevents tearing: two components in one render seeing different values.

question: Why can't hooks be called conditionally, but use() can?
shortAnswer: Regular hooks store state in a per-component list indexed by call order, so skipping one shifts every later hook to the wrong slot. use() does not allocate a slot — it reads a promise or context and either returns the value or suspends. With nothing positional to preserve, calling it conditionally is safe.
memoryHook: Hooks own a numbered slot. use() owns none, so it can appear anywhere — including inside an if.
answer:
## Why regular hooks are positional React keeps a list per component and walks it in order on every render. Nothing identifies a hook except its index: ```jsx useState('') // slot 0 useState(0) // slot 1 useEffect(…) // slot 2 ``` Skip slot 1 on one render and slot 2's data ends up read as slot 1's. React detects the count change and throws. --- ## What `use` does instead ```jsx import { use } from 'react'; function Comments({ commentsPromise, showComments }) { if (!showComments) return null; const comments = use(commentsPromise); // ✅ legal after an early return return
    {comments.map((c) =>
  • {c.text}
    • )}
; } ``` `use` does not persist anything between renders. It either: - **Resolves** — the promise is already settled, so it returns the value, or - **Suspends** — throws to the nearest `` boundary, which shows the fallback and retries when the promise settles No slot, no ordering requirement. --- ## What it works with ```jsx const data = use(promise); // suspends until resolved const theme = use(ThemeContext); // like useContext, but conditional ``` That second form is genuinely useful — reading a context only in one branch was previously impossible. --- ## The trap ```jsx // ❌ New promise every render → suspends forever, refetching in a loop function Profile({ id }) { const user = use(fetch(`/api/users/${id}`).then((r) => r.json())); } ``` The promise must come from somewhere stable — created in a Server Component and passed as a prop, or cached by a data library. `use` consumes promises; it does not manage them. --- ## Why the naming is deliberate It is `use`, not `useSomething`. The React team chose a name that does not read like a standard hook, precisely because the rules are different. The lint rule knows about it and does not apply the ordering check. > This question separates people who memorised "never call hooks conditionally" from people who know *why* the rule exists. If you can explain the slot mechanism, the `use` exception follows naturally.
